````text
1	# Google Docs reference
2	
3	As a first step, before you create a Google Doc or change one, you must read the design rules below in full: how a document should look and read, and how to edit one. After them, "Applying the design rules" says how to carry out the rules with these tools, and the rest of the file covers the Docs connector's `read_doc` and `update_doc` and the Drive tools that help with Docs.
4	
5	# Document design
6	
7	When the user asks for something specific, such as a font, a color, a length or a structure, do that; these rules decide what the user left open. The rules for the text itself are under Writing, and the rules for changing a document that already exists are under Editing an existing document.
8	
9	## Structure
10	
11	- **Plan the sections before you write, and merge any two that answer the same question in different words.** If the user asked for a set number of sections, replace the merged one with a section that covers something new.
12	- **Each section appears once.** Before you finish, read the headings in order and check that none is repeated.
13	- **An executive summary opens with the conclusion.** Its first paragraph states what the reader should believe or do. Numbers belong in the body sections, where they support the conclusion; they are not the conclusion. "$1.2B total debt across 7 instruments, weighted-average coupon 4.8%" is data. "Refinancing risk is concentrated in 2027. We recommend an opportunistic tender for the 2027 notes given the current cash position" is a conclusion. A summary that is only a list of numbers has not stated a conclusion.
14	- **A length the user gave is a limit.** "Three pages", "one page" or "500 words" is a hard constraint: check it before you finish and cut if you are over. Five pages for a three-page request is a defect, not thoroughness. Count the pages in the rendered document; without a render, estimate about 3,000 characters per page.
15	- **Limits still apply after the first request.** A length or a set of sources the user gave at the start still holds when a later request doesn't repeat it.
16	- **Numbers and quotes taken from a source match the source.** Take every figure, quote and page reference from a part of the source you have actually read, not from memory. If you can't find a value, say so instead of estimating it.
17	
18	## Styles
19	
20	The look of a document comes from its styles: the Normal text style for body text and the built-in heading styles for headings. Formatting set directly on individual paragraphs carries over into the text added after them and spreads across a long document.
21	
22	- **Set the body font once, for the whole body**, not on each paragraph or run. A font set paragraph by paragraph misses the paragraphs added later, and the document ends up in two fonts.
23	- **Headings use the heading styles.** Never make a heading out of bold, larger body text: it is missing from the table of contents and the outline, and its formatting carries over into the next paragraph.
24	- **Don't resize a single heading.** Each heading level already has its own size, and an override on one paragraph can make a subsection look like a section. If a heading is at the wrong level, change its level. If every heading at one level should be smaller, change that heading style. Don't move a correctly placed heading to a lower level only to make it smaller.
25	- **New content of the same kind takes the style around it; new content of a different kind does not.** A clause added next to other clauses gets their style. A table or a body paragraph added right after a list item or a heading gets the Normal text style, without the heading's bold. Otherwise the table cells get list markers and the body text comes out bold or as a heading.
26	- **Color goes on a phrase, not on a section.** One sentence in red is emphasis. Three paragraphs in red is too much, and the reader stops reading the color as a signal. If you want to color more than one paragraph, you need a heading or a callout box instead. Color the words themselves, not the whole paragraph, so the color doesn't carry over into the next paragraph.
27	
28	## Fonts
29	
30	- **New legal documents use Times New Roman.** When you draft a contract, brief, motion, legal memo or legal letter from scratch, with no template, set the body in Times New Roman. It is the professional default in legal practice, and other fonts read as informal. This doesn't apply when the document already has content (use its body font), when a template sets the font, or when the user names a font.
31	
32	## Lists and numbering
33	
34	- **Never type list markers or section numbers** in a new document, or in a list or heading the document numbers automatically. In those, don't write "•", "-", "*", "1.", "3.2" or "(a)" as text; use the document's list and heading numbering. Typed markers look right until someone inserts an item or a section above them, and then the numbers are wrong.
35	- **List items directly next to each other with the same list style join one list.** Numbering can also continue across a paragraph between two lists, so when a second numbered list should start again at 1, check that it does.
36	
37	## Tables
38	
39	- **Match the existing tables.** When the document already has tables, give a new one the same borders, fills and header row. One table with a colored header among three plain ones looks like a mistake.
40	
41	## Page layout
42	
43	- **Leave the page setup as it is unless the user asks**, and in a pageless document skip the rules below about pages and columns. "Applying the design rules" says how to recognize one.
44	- **Keep each heading on the same page as the paragraph after it.** A heading alone at the bottom of a page reads as broken even when the content is right. In a document you create, set "keep with next" on the heading styles, so it applies to every heading; in an existing document, do it when you find a heading separated from its paragraph.
45	- **To keep a section on one page, such as a financial statement, start it on a new page with one page break before its heading.** Check for an existing break first: a second one only adds a blank page. If the section still splits with a break in front of it, it is longer than a page; say so instead of adding another break.
46	- **When a table is longer than a page, stop its rows from breaking across pages**, so that each row is whole on one page.
47	- **Page numbers are fields, not typed text.** "Page 1" typed into a footer reads 1 on every page.
48	- **Headers and footers can have variants.** If the document has a different first-page header, or different headers on odd and even pages, each one is separate: change every one that applies.
49	- **Columns belong to a section, not to a paragraph style.** To set part of a document in two columns, give that part its own section.
50	- **Use real footnotes, not [1] markers typed into the text.**
51	
52	## Check the result
53	
54	Look at the rendered pages, not only the text. Assume there are formatting problems and look for them:
55	
56	- **Fonts:** a paragraph in a different font from the rest, or a size change in the middle of a section.
57	- **Styles:** added text that looks like plain body text where the paragraphs around it are headings or styled body text.
58	- **Numbering:** a list item that lost its marker, or (a) (b) that restarted as (1) (2).
59	- **Tables:** columns that changed width, or cells that wrap where they didn't before.
60	- **Formatting that runs on:** bold or italic that continues past where it should stop.
61	- **Spacing:** double blank lines, a paragraph pressed against the one above it, uneven indents. In a doc that started blank, blocks added with Docs edit requests touch unless you set the space between them; the "Add space between blocks" recipe says how.
62	- **Suggestions:** insertions and deletions that render garbled or overlap the normal text.
63	- **Page breaks:** a heading alone at the bottom of a page, a blank page, a section that used to fit on one page and now splits.
64	
65	After you fix one problem, check the paragraphs and pages around it. A fix to one paragraph often changes the next one, and a change in length moves the page breaks.
66	
67	## Writing
68	
69	Text you write in a document should read as though a person wrote it. When readers think something was written by AI, they judge it as sloppy and stop trusting it, whatever the content. They make that judgment from a set of common indicators, listed below, so take extra care to keep them out of your writing. These rules are for text you write, and a style the user or their style guide asks for takes priority. Do not rewrite the user's existing text to follow them unless the user asks you to.
70	
71	- Say what is true without first denying something else. "Revenue grew 12%, three times the US rate," not "This isn't a growth story, it's a market-share story." Do not open a paragraph or bullet with "Here's the thing" or "The real story is".
72	- Match the number of bullets, examples, and adjectives to the content, not to a default of three. Two drivers get two bullets; five get five. A list of exactly three ("fast, reliable, and scalable") usually means the third item was added for rhythm, not because there were three things to say, and readers read it as filler.
73	- Do not use a metaphor where a literal word will do. If a plain description exists ("the same construction," "the same pattern," "slowed," "fell"), use it. Metaphors are for when the literal version would be longer or less precise, which is rare in analytical writing. Test: if the metaphor can be replaced by a plain word without losing meaning, replace it. A metaphor makes the reader translate it back into the plain claim and carries meaning you did not choose. The ones that appear most are "north star", "move the needle", "double-click" (meaning look closer), "unpack", "journey", and "landscape" (meaning a market). Common ones in business writing: "moat", "headwind", "drag" (meaning a cost on results), "safety net", "clears the bar", and "land" meaning finish or total ("lands $4.4k under budget"). Examples:
74	  - Bad: "The ones it has are the same species." Good: "The ones it has follow the same pattern."
75	  - Bad: "A coordinated digestion pause would be visible immediately." Good: "If several large customers cut capex in the same quarter, it would show up in the next guide."
76	  - Bad: "Architecture transitions compressed margin on the way in and expanded it on the way out." Good: "Gross margin fell during the Hopper-to-Blackwell ramp and recovered once Blackwell shipped at volume."
77	  - Bad: "The lever that unlocks growth." Good: "The pricing change is what makes the target reachable."
78	- Cut words that claim importance without giving evidence: "genuinely", "truly", "actually", "clearly", "significantly", "robust", "leverage", "delve", "actionable insights", "learnings". Where one of them stood in for a fact, put the fact there ("margins fell 4 points", not "margins fell significantly"); otherwise delete it. When "leverage" or "significant" carries its financial or statistical meaning ("net leverage", "statistically significant"), it is a literal term; keep it.
79	- Use full stops and commas, and a colon before a list. No emoji in the document.
80	- Use em dashes sparingly: at most one in a paragraph, and none in a heading, a title, or between a bold label and the text after it. Several em dashes in one paragraph is one of the first things readers use to spot machine writing. In place of one, use a comma, a colon, parentheses, or a new sentence, not an en dash or a spaced hyphen.
81	- Headings in the document are about the content, not about your process: "Europe missed plan by $1.9M" or "Pricing", not "What I changed" or "The hard part". Standard labels such as "Executive Summary" or "Next steps" are fine. When the document already has headings, phrase new ones the same way, for example as short labels or as full sentences.
82	- Keep the conversation out of the document. When the user asks for a shorter or more formal version, make it shorter or more formal; do not title it "Executive Summary (Condensed)" or open it with "Updated per your feedback". The document's readers did not see the request, so those lines mean nothing to them. Say what changed in your reply, not in the document. This covers the document's text, not replies in comment threads.
83	
84	## Editing an existing document
85	
86	These rules apply whenever you change a document that already exists. Everything you add also follows the rules above.
87	
88	### Change only what was asked
89	
90	- **Match the scope of the edit to the request.** "Fill in this section" means add text. It doesn't mean also changing the alignment, adding underlining, reformatting tables or restyling nearby paragraphs. If a check shows a formatting change you didn't intend, undo it.
91	- **Change the smallest range that covers the change.** Replace the words that change, not the paragraph or section around them. Never delete and rebuild a paragraph, a section or the document to change part of it: that loses comments, bookmarks, images, charts and other embedded objects.
92	- **Keep the original wording wherever you aren't deliberately changing it.** Rewording the user didn't ask for is one more change they have to find and review. In a contract it is a substantive change: "aggregate" becoming "total", or "shall not" becoming "will not", changes what the text says.
93	- **Reformat by role.** "Make the body text 11pt" means the body text, not the headings; "indent the section headers" means the headings. Pick out the paragraphs by their style before you change them.
94	- **Take target values from the document, not from a guess.** If one table's header row is wrong and three others are right, copy the values from a correct one. When the user points at a reference ("make it look like section 3"), read that section's exact style, font, size, color, alignment and line spacing, and apply those. A guessed 18pt in a document built at 11pt is worse than the original problem.
95	- **Keep similar tables consistent, but only when the user asked you to reformat tables.** When the user asks you to reformat one of several similar tables, make the same change to the others or tell the user you changed only the one.
96	- **A table that changed as a side effect of another edit is a mistake to undo**, not a change to copy to the other tables.
97	- **Never replace a bare number across the whole document.** Closing a gap in section numbers by replacing every "7" with "6" also changes a "7.1x" interest coverage, a "7.5%" coupon and "FY2027". Renumber the headings one at a time.
98	
99	### Match what is there
100	
101	- **Text you add uses the document's body font and style**, not the editor's default. After you insert text, check its font and size against the paragraph before it.
102	- **Use the document's spelling variety**, for example British or American English. Keep new text in the variety the document already uses, never mix varieties in one document, and don't change existing text to another variety unless the user asks. If the document has no text yet, follow the variety of the user's messages.
103	- **Set explicit colors from the document.** If you must set a text color, copy it from an existing body paragraph instead of assuming black: many document styles use a dark gray or a theme color.
104	- **New numbered headings get their number from the document.** When the document numbers its headings automatically, write the heading text without a number and give the heading the same style or list level as the headings next to it, so it takes the next number. If the document numbers its headings by hand, follow that convention instead.
105	- **New list items continue the list.** Add an item as part of the list it belongs to, and check that it took the next marker: (b) after (a), not a second (a) or a skipped letter.
106	- **Making headings consistent.** When the user asks for all the headings to match, first give any hand-formatted heading (bold, larger body text) the right heading style. Then set each level to the font of its own heading style, one level at a time; applying the first level's font to every level removes the difference between levels. Applying a heading style doesn't remove a size or color set directly on the text, so clear those as well.
107	
108	### Things inside the text
109	
110	Some elements sit inside a paragraph's text without looking like separate objects: footnote marks, chips (such as a person, date or file chip), bookmark boundaries, comment anchors, and inline images and charts. Replacing or deleting a range that contains one removes it: the footnote is gone, the chip is deleted, the bookmark moves, the chart disappears.
111	
112	- **Before you edit a sentence, check what is inside it**, and change the text on either side of such an element rather than through it.
113	- **A paragraph with no visible text can still hold an image or a chart**, and a floating shape is anchored to a paragraph. Deleting the paragraph deletes them, so check before you delete an empty-looking paragraph.
114	- **In a section set in columns, edit the text inside the section.** Don't remove the section break that holds the column setting.
115	
116	### Templates
117	
118	- **Fill the placeholders and keep the structure.** Never delete an image placeholder or a signature line while filling a template; removing one breaks the template for the next person who uses it.
119	- **Find every placeholder before you fill any.** Templates often use typed markers such as [CLIENT NAME]. If a template has none, find each section by its heading and write after it.
120	
121	### Comments
122	
123	- **Reply in the thread.** When you respond to a comment, reply to it; don't start a new comment. If your tool can't reply to comments, give the user the reply text to paste into each thread.
124	- **One thread per topic.** Before you add a comment, look for an existing thread on the same text or topic, including one you left earlier, and reply there. Several comments stacked on one paragraph make it unclear which note is current.
125	- **Leave comments where they are.** Don't delete or resolve a comment unless the user asks. Reply once per comment; don't add a second reply that says nothing new.
126	- **When you edit commented text, change words inside the commented range, not all of it.** A comment is attached to its text, and replacing all of that text deletes the comment and its replies. Make the edit first and reply after it, so that no reply describes an edit that didn't happen.
127	- **"Address the comments" means every comment.** Handle each one: make the edit it asks for, if any, reply with a one-line note, and leave the thread open unless the user asks you to resolve it.
128	
129	### Suggestions
130	
131	- **Use real suggestions**, never strikethrough and colored text made to look like them. The reviewer needs to accept or reject each change.
132	- **Don't accept or reject changes, or delete comments, to clean up.** In a review, the suggestions and comment threads are the work product: accepting them erases the record of what changed, and deleting comments erases the reviewers' notes. "Clean up the document" means fix the formatting. Accept, reject or delete only the ones the user names.
133	- **Mark only the words that change.** A paragraph replaced as a whole shows as the whole paragraph deleted and inserted again, and the reviewer can't see what changed. Replace only the words that change, and make several small changes in one paragraph as separate edits. To change a cap from twelve months to six, the change is "twelve (12)" to "six (6)", not the sentence it sits in.
134	
135	### After structural changes
136	
137	- **Keep the table of contents current.** After you add, remove or rename a heading in a document that has a table of contents, update it in the same step: a table of contents that lists "Section 4: Risk Factors" when section 4 is now "Liquidity" is a visible defect. Update an existing one; don't add one the document doesn't have unless the user asks for it. If your tool can't update it, tell the user it needs updating.
138	- **Remove everything in a section you delete.** Deleting a section's paragraphs can leave its table or images behind. Count the tables before and after, and check the count dropped by the number you removed.
139	- **Before removing a duplicate section, read both copies.** Keep the one whose formatting matches the rest of the document, and tell the user which one you kept and why.
140	- **Clear what deletions leave behind:** empty tables, two or more blank paragraphs in a row (collapse them to one), list items cut off from their list, and blank paragraphs at the end that push an empty last page.
141	
142	### Check your edits
143	
144	After each edit, read back what you changed: the text, its style, its font and any list marker. After an edit that can move the layout, such as added or removed content, a table or formatting change, or a fix to something that looked wrong, also check the rendered pages, including the pages around the change, against the list under Check the result above.
145	
146	# Docs and Drive tools
147	
148	## Applying the design rules
149	
150	Some of the design rules above act on a named style (Normal text, Heading 1 to 6) or on a page-number field, and the Docs API can apply a named style but not change one, and can't insert a page number. Others depend on the page setup. Do this instead:
151	
152	- **Body font, such as Times New Roman for a new legal draft:** set it once over the whole body with `updateTextStyle` (`weightedFontFamily`, `fields: "weightedFontFamily"`) after the text is in, and give text you add later the same font.
153	- **Keep each heading with the next paragraph:** set `keepWithNext: true` on each heading paragraph with `updateParagraphStyle` (`fields: "keepWithNext"`).
154	- **Make every heading at one level smaller or larger:** tell the user they can resize one heading at that level and then choose Format > Paragraph styles > Heading N > Update 'Heading N' to match, which changes the style itself. If they want you to do it instead, set the same size on every heading at that level in one batch.
155	- **Page numbers:** tell the user to add them with Insert > Page numbers.
156	- **Whether a tab is pageless:** in the `read_doc` result, check the tab you are editing. It is pageless when `documentFormat.documentMode` is `PAGELESS` in its `documentTab.documentStyle`, or in the top-level `documentStyle` when there is no `tabs` key. In a pageless tab, don't add page numbers, headers, footers or columns; tell the user to switch it to pages first, with Format > Switch to Pages format.
157	- **Page setup, when the user asks for a change:** send `updateDocumentStyle` with `tabId` on the request itself (it has no location or range), the new values in `documentStyle`, and only those field names in `fields`, without the `documentStyle.` prefix: `{"updateDocumentStyle": {"tabId": "t.0", "documentStyle": {"marginTop": {"magnitude": 54, "unit": "PT"}}, "fields": "marginTop"}}`. A field named in `fields` but missing from `documentStyle` is cleared, so never use `*`, which names every field.
158	
159	These are based on the Docs API reference and have not been tested through the connector.
160	
161	## Create
162	
163	Call Drive `create_file` with `contentMimeType: "text/html"` and the document as `textContent`. Drive converts `<h1>`, `<h2>`, `<p>`, `<ul>`, `<ol>`, `<b>`, `<i>`, and `<a>` into native Docs formatting. This is much faster and less error-prone than building a new doc with Docs edit requests. Use the Docs connector for changes after that. For a Word file the user will download rather than edit in Google Docs, use the `docx` skill instead.
164	
165	## How a doc is addressed
166	
167	Every Docs edit points at a position, so the model of positions matters more than anything else in this section.
168	
169	- **Indexes are UTF-16 code units** counted from the start of a tab's body, which starts at index 1. A character outside the Basic Multilingual Plane, such as 🙂, counts as 2, and an emoji built from several characters counts as more: 👍🏽 (👍 plus a skin tone) is 4. Docs refuses an insert inside an emoji with "The insertion index cannot be within a grapheme cluster", and a delete through the middle of 🙂 with "Invalid deletion range". Every paragraph ends with a newline that occupies one index.
170	- **Every insert or delete shifts everything after it.** Requests in one `update_doc` call run in order, so an index computed from the read is only valid for the first request that touches that region. Order the requests from the highest index to the lowest, and no request moves a position a later request relies on.
171	- **Indexes go stale after any write.** Never reuse indexes from a read taken before your last write. Read again, then compute.
172	- **Guard every batch with the revision, unless it is only `replaceAllText`.** Pass the `revisionId` from a read taken after your last write as `writeControl.requiredRevisionId`. If someone edited the doc in between, the whole batch is rejected with a 400 instead of landing in the wrong place. On that error, read again and recompute. Do not retry without the guard.
173	- **Tabs are separate index spaces.** A doc can have several tabs, and child tabs under them. Every `location` and `range` takes a `tabId`; without it, the request applies to the first tab, which is a silent failure when the user meant another one. A pasted URL like `.../edit?tab=t.abc123` names the tab: `t.abc123` is the `tabId`. `replaceAllText` is the opposite: without `tabsCriteria` it changes every tab, child tabs included, and naming a parent tab in `tabsCriteria` does not include its child tabs.
174	- **Pending suggestions are in the index space.** `read_doc` returns suggested insertions and deletions inline, as text runs that carry `suggestedInsertionIds` or `suggestedDeletionIds`, and they occupy real indexes. Don't treat a suggested deletion as live text, and don't insert inside one.
175	- **The body's final newline can't be deleted.** To append, insert at the last element's `endIndex - 1`.
176	
177	## Read
178	
179	There are two reads, and they serve different purposes.
180	
181	- **Drive `read_file_content`** returns the doc as Markdown: headings, tables, and bold, typically a few KB. Use it first to understand what the doc says and to find the text you'll anchor on. Pass `includeComments: true`; without it, emoji come out garbled and the end of the text is cut off. With it, commented text sits inside `<comment_start id=…>` and `<comment_end id=…>` tags whose id matches a listed comment; keep the tags out of find text. It is not the index space: it escapes Markdown characters, and it glues pending suggestions to the text around them. Never compute an index from it.
182	- **Docs `read_doc`** returns the full `documents.get` JSON: every element with its `startIndex` and `endIndex`, every style, the `revisionId`, and the tabs. Use it when an edit needs indexes. It is large: a two-page doc with one table can exceed 100 KB. Pass `commentsIncluded: true` only when you need comments; it has returned each comment with its place in the text. If the result shows `COMMENTS_VIEW_MODE_OMITTED` instead, read them with Drive `read_file_content` and `includeComments: true`, or ask the user to paste the ones they want handled.
183	
184	Where the content lives in the `read_doc` JSON:
185	
186	```
187	revisionId
188	tabs[].tabProperties.tabId
189	tabs[].documentTab.body.content[]          body elements, in order
190	  .paragraph.elements[].textRun.content    text, with startIndex / endIndex on the element
191	  .paragraph.paragraphStyle.namedStyleType HEADING_1, NORMAL_TEXT, ...
192	  .table.tableRows[].tableCells[].content[]  each cell holds its own paragraphs
193	tabs[].childTabs[]                          nested tabs, same shape
194	```
195	
196	If the doc has no `tabs` key, the body is at the top level: `body.content[]`.
197	
198	### Use the helper script for positions
199	
200	`scripts/docs_index.py` (in this skill's folder) reads the `read_doc` JSON from a file and prints only what an edit needs. Where you can run code, use it rather than walking the JSON by eye. That walk is where index errors come from.
201	
202	- A large `read_doc` result may be saved to a file, and the result then gives the path. Run the script on that path.
203	- If the JSON came back in context and the doc is small, read the positions from it directly.
204	- If the read was cut off and not saved anywhere, don't guess positions. Use `replaceAllText`, which needs none, when the find text matches only the text you mean to change (add neighboring words until it does), or tell the user the doc is too large to edit by position here.
205	
206	Commands:
207	
208	```
209	python <skill>/scripts/docs_index.py outline DOC.json
210	    one line per element: index range, style, table cell position, text.
211	    Pending suggestions show as [+inserted] / [-deleted].
212	    Ends with the body end index for appends.
213	python <skill>/scripts/docs_index.py find DOC.json "exact text"
214	    index range of every match within one paragraph, whether it is bold, and whether it sits
215	    in a pending suggestion. A match can't cross a non-text element, such as a chip, image or footnote mark.
216	python <skill>/scripts/docs_index.py fill-table DOC.json --table N --data rows.json [--bold-header]
217	    the full update_doc arguments (requests + writeControl) to fill empty table N, the
218	    TABLE #N that outline prints (every tab and nested table is counted), from a JSON list of rows.
219	python <skill>/scripts/docs_index.py new-table --at I --data rows.json --revision REV [--tab T] [--bold-header]
220	    the full update_doc arguments to insert a table at I, the endIndex - 1 of the paragraph
221	    it goes after, and fill it in the same call. Needs no DOC.json.
222	```
223	
224	outline and find print the `revisionId` and the tab ID; fill-table puts the `revisionId` in its `writeControl`.
225	
226	## Edit recipes
227	
228	Each recipe is one `update_doc` call. Add `tabId` to every `location` and `range` when the doc has more than one tab, and add `writeControl: {"requiredRevisionId": ...}` to every call except one made only of `replaceAllText` requests. Put real newlines in inserted text, not an escaped `\n`.
229	
230	**Change a word or phrase.** `replaceAllText` needs no read and no indexes:
231	
232	```json
233	{"replaceAllText": {"containsText": {"text": "Q3 launch", "matchCase": true},
234	  "replaceText": "Q4 launch", "tabsCriteria": {"tabIds": ["t.0"]}}}
235	```
236	
237	The reply reports `occurrencesChanged`. Zero means the text didn't match exactly: check it against `read_file_content`, but remember that file escapes characters like `&` and `*`. The replacement takes the style of the first character it replaces, so replacing a span that starts in bold makes the whole replacement bold. If that matters, start the find on an unstyled character, or check the result with `find` afterward. It changes every match in the tabs it covers (every tab unless `tabsCriteria` names some), so use it when every match should change, such as a date or a name the user wants changed throughout. When only one occurrence should change, or the find text is short enough to occur inside unrelated text (a bare number such as "7", a common word), delete and insert at the range `find` gives for that occurrence. Never put a paragraph's trailing newline in the find text: the replaced paragraph can take the next paragraph's style (a body paragraph becomes a heading), or the next paragraph can lose its heading style.
238	
239	**Rewrite a paragraph.** Take its `startIndex` and `endIndex` from `outline`. Delete `[start, end - 1]`, which keeps the paragraph's newline and style, then insert at `start`:
240	
241	```json
242	[{"deleteContentRange": {"range": {"startIndex": 120, "endIndex": 184}}},
243	 {"insertText": {"location": {"index": 120}, "text": "New paragraph text."}}]
244	```
245	
246	For several paragraphs, do the highest one first. When only some words in the paragraph change, delete and insert only those words at the range `find` gives, not the whole paragraph. A footnote mark, chip or image elsewhere in the paragraph then stays, and in suggestion mode the suggestion shows only the words that changed. To delete a whole paragraph, delete `[start, end]`. In three cases that range is refused, with "Invalid deletion range" or "The range cannot include the newline character at the end of the segment"; use these ranges instead. For the doc's last paragraph, delete from the previous paragraph's `endIndex - 1` to the last paragraph's `endIndex - 1`. For the paragraph just before a table, and for a table cell's only paragraph, delete the text only, `[start, end - 1]`; an empty paragraph stays, because Google keeps one before every table and in every cell.
247	
248	**Append to the end.** Insert at the body end index minus 1 that `outline` prints. Start the text with a newline to begin a new paragraph. The new paragraph takes the named style of the one it splits from, so after a heading, set it to `NORMAL_TEXT` with `updateParagraphStyle`.
249	
250	**Insert new paragraphs with styles.** Insert the text, then style ranges you compute from the insert point and the text length (in UTF-16 units). Headings use `updateParagraphStyle` with `namedStyleType` `HEADING_1` to `HEADING_6`, `TITLE`, or `NORMAL_TEXT` and `fields: "namedStyleType"`. Lists use `createParagraphBullets` over the range with a `bulletPreset` such as `BULLET_DISC_CIRCLE_SQUARE` or `NUMBERED_DECIMAL_ALPHA_ROMAN`. Typing "- " or "1. " makes text, not a list, and `createParagraphBullets` over typed markers keeps them as text, so delete them first. For nesting, put one leading tab per nesting level at the start of each nested line, before the first `createParagraphBullets`. It turns the tabs into levels and removes them, which shifts every later index by the number of tabs. Bulleting a paragraph directly after a list, with the same preset, adds it to that list. Inserted text takes the style of the text before it, or at the start of a paragraph the style of that paragraph's first character, so reset bold and italic on new body text with `updateTextStyle` (`fields: "bold,italic"`, empty `textStyle`). Don't reset headings, because that removes their bold.
251	
252	**Add space between blocks.** In a doc that had content before you started, set space only on the paragraphs you add, and match how its own paragraphs are spaced, unless the user asks otherwise. By default, a new blank doc's Normal text has no space above or below it, so the paragraphs, lists, tables and code blocks you add to one with `update_doc` run together. Set the space with `updateParagraphStyle`, last, after the text, named styles and bullets: `spaceBelow` of about 8pt on each body paragraph, on the last item of each list and on the last line of an unshaded code block, and the same `spaceAbove` on body text right after a table or a shaded block. Headings bring their own space. Name only what you set in `fields`, never `*`: a field named there but missing from `paragraphStyle` is reset.
253	
254	```json
255	{"updateParagraphStyle": {"range": {"startIndex": 120, "endIndex": 184},
256	  "paragraphStyle": {"spaceBelow": {"magnitude": 8, "unit": "PT"}}, "fields": "spaceBelow"}}
257	```
258	
259	Set space last because a `NORMAL_TEXT` request on a paragraph that is already Normal text can clear it, and a paragraph split from a spaced one copies it. The empty paragraph Google adds after a table is already a blank line: leave it with no extra space, or put the next text in it and set `spaceAbove` there. Keep the lines of a code block tight: `updateParagraphStyle` styles every paragraph its range overlaps, table cells included, so don't use one range over the whole doc. Docs draws the space above and below a shaded paragraph, such as a line of a shaded code block, in the shading's color, so space set there makes no white gap. In a new blank doc, don't add empty paragraphs as spacers: one added after a list item or a heading can come out as an empty list item or heading.
260	
261	**Add a table with content.** One call, with no second read. Place the table after a paragraph, at that paragraph's `endIndex - 1`: for a table under a heading, that is the last paragraph of the section, or the heading itself if the section is empty. Never use the start of a heading: that leaves an empty heading above the table, the heading's font in its cells, and, with `new-table`, the heading itself turned into body text. Write the rows to a JSON file and run:
262	
263	```
264	python <skill>/scripts/docs_index.py new-table --at <endIndex - 1> --data rows.json --revision <revisionId> [--tab <tabId>] [--bold-header]
265	```
266	
267	Pass its output as the `requests` and `writeControl` of one `update_doc` call. It inserts the table, fills the cells, bolds the header row with `--bold-header`, and sets the empty paragraph Google adds after the table to `NORMAL_TEXT` (otherwise, after a heading, it becomes an empty heading). Pass `--tab` whenever the doc has more than one tab; without it every request goes to the first tab. The command needs only the index, the revisionId and the tabId, which you can read from `read_doc` even when the result came back in the chat rather than as a file.
268	
269	Without the script, put the same requests in one batch: `insertTable` at index `i` makes a table that starts at `i + 1`; in an R x C table, cell (r, c)'s text goes at `i + 4 + r × (2C + 1) + 2c`, and the empty paragraph after the table is at `i + 3 + R × (2C + 1)` until you insert text, so put its `NORMAL_TEXT` reset right after `insertTable`. Fill from the last cell to the first, so each insert only shifts cells already filled.
270	
271	To fill a table that already exists, a cell's text goes at its first paragraph's `startIndex`, which is the cell's own `startIndex + 1`; Google rejects an insert at the cell's `startIndex` ("The insertion index must be inside the bounds of an existing paragraph"). With a saved read, `fill-table` builds these requests; it assumes the cells are empty.
272	
273	**Change table structure.** `insertTableRow`, `deleteTableRow`, `insertTableColumn`, and `deleteTableColumn` take `tableCellLocation: {"tableStartLocation": {"index": <table startIndex>}, "rowIndex": r, "columnIndex": c}`. `updateTableCellStyle` sets cell backgrounds over a `tableRange` built from the same location plus `rowSpan` and `columnSpan`. Colors use `rgbColor` values from 0 to 1. A row inserted below a bold header row comes out bold, a new column copies its neighbor's width and background, and `unmergeTableCells` leaves all of the merged text in the first cell. To delete a whole table, delete exactly `[table startIndex, table endIndex]`.
274	
275	**Suggest instead of edit.** Add `"writeMode": "SUGGEST"` to `writeControl`, and the same requests land as tracked suggestions that the doc's owner can accept or reject. Use it when the user asks for suggestions, redlines, tracked changes, or a review, or when the doc belongs to someone else and the user wants to propose rather than change. You can't accept or reject suggestions through the API, so tell the user they're waiting in the doc. Before you tell them, read the doc again with `read_doc` and run `outline`: inserted and deleted text should show as `[+...]` or `[-...]` (outline doesn't show suggested formatting changes). If new text shows as plain text, or deleted text is gone instead of showing as `[-...]`, the change was made directly; say so, and don't call it a suggestion. Suggested deletions stay in the index space until someone resolves them; see "How a doc is addressed". The connector has answered this mode with "Unsupported WriteControl mode". If it does, make no direct edits in its place: tell the user suggestions aren't available, and offer to list the proposed changes in your reply or to edit directly.
276	
277	```json
278	{"documentId": "...", "requests": [...],
279	 "writeControl": {"writeMode": "SUGGEST", "requiredRevisionId": "..."}}
280	```
281	
282	**Tabs.** `addDocumentTab` with `tabProperties.title` creates a tab, and the reply holds its `tabId`. `updateDocumentTabProperties` renames one (`fields: "title"`), and `deleteTab` removes one along with its child tabs, but not the only tab. Set `tabProperties.parentTabId` to create a child tab; tabs nest at most three levels deep. A new tab starts with one empty paragraph, so its first insert index is 1.
283	
284	**Add a footnote.** `createFootnote` returns the footnote's ID; the new footnote holds a single space. In the next call, add your text with `insertText` and `endOfSegmentLocation: {"segmentId": "<footnote ID>"}`, then delete the space with `deleteContentRange` over `{"segmentId": "<footnote ID>", "startIndex": 0, "endIndex": 1}`. Drive's text read leaves footnote text out; check it with `read_doc`.
285	
286	## Verify
287	
288	- For content, read with Drive `read_file_content` and `includeComments: true`, and check the text you changed.
289	- For positions and styles, read with `read_doc` and run `outline` or `find` on the result. `find` shows whether replaced text picked up bold, and whether a match sits in a pending suggestion.
290	- For layout, where you can run code, export with Drive `download_file_content` and `exportMimeType: "application/pdf"`, then run `python <skill>/scripts/render_export.py <saved export> <out dir>` and check the page images against the list under "Check the result" above. If the export comes back in the chat instead of being saved to a file, skip the render rather than copying it into a file. If you can't run code, skipped the render, or it failed, rely on the two checks above and tell the user you couldn't check the layout visually.
291	
292	## Docs failures
293	
294	| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
295	|---|---|---|
296	| `read_doc` result too large or cut off | Full document JSON for a long or table-heavy doc | Orient with Drive `read_file_content`. Use `replaceAllText` where the find text matches only the text you mean to change (add neighboring words until it does). If the result was saved to a file, run `docs_index.py` on it. |
297	| An edit landed in the wrong tab | No `tabId` in the location or range | Add the `tabId` from the read or from the URL's `?tab=` value. |
298	| `replaceAllText` changed other tabs | No `tabsCriteria` | Scope it with `tabsCriteria.tabIds`. |
299	| `replaceAllText` reports 0 occurrences | Find text copied from `read_file_content`, which escapes `&`, `*`, and similar characters, tags commented text, or glues suggestions | Use the literal text, or check it with `docs_index.py find`. |
300	| Text shows as "RBRunning back" | A pending suggestion read as plain text | Read with `read_doc`. `outline` marks suggested text as `[+...]` and `[-...]`. |
301	| A heading loses its bold after an edit | A style reset was applied to the heading | Reset styles only on body text. |
302	| Replaced text turned bold | The replacement inherited the style of the first replaced character | Clear it with `updateTextStyle` over the new range. |
303	| Edits land in the wrong place | Requests ran from the lowest index to the highest, or used indexes from before an earlier write | Order requests from the highest index to the lowest, and read again after every write. |
304	| Typed "- " shows as text, not a bullet | Lists are paragraph properties | Delete the typed markers, then use `createParagraphBullets` over the range. Bulleting keeps typed markers as text. |
305

289	Requirements and Design
290	kojoshuay
291	-
292	The primary design dilemma was determining the most efficient database architecture to
293	store a single site-wide security boolean without introducing unnecessary technical debt.
294	-
295	Adding a new boolean column to the Deployment table was rejected because it
296	would require building new repository methods, endpoints, and admin checks
297	from scratch.
298	-
299	Creating a SiteSettings table was rejected as over-engineering since a single
300	boolean setting does not justify building a new schema, repository, and DI
301	container.
302	-
303	Storing the setting as a row in the existing Feature table was chosen because it
304	requires zero schema changes and safely reuses the application's established
305	backend architecture for site-wide rules.
306	zachbowden
307	-
308	For the soft cancellation feature, we chose a five-minute window before a cancellation
309	actually goes through. That gives the user enough time to reconsider without leaving the
310	￼
311	￼
312	host uncertain for long. During that window, the host's panel still shows the booking as
313	active, and it disappears only once the five minutes are up. For the waitlist feature, we
314	chose to give a user six hours to accept an offered spot. That is enough time for them to
315	work out whether they can attend, and for the host to adjust their plans for the meeting.
316	We also decided to support both whole-day and specific-time waitlists, each used in
317	different situations. The whole-day option appears only when every time slot that day is
318	booked, and on any other day users see a waitlist option for each booked time.

=== checkin
# Sprint 3 mid-sprint check-in: zach-short

**Code PR:** TODO: link the #130 PR here before Nov 12, 11:59 PM (it must be open and ready for review, or merged).

## What have you implemented so far, and what remains?

So far my Sprint 3 work is planning. For the team feature, #131 (OIDC sign-in), I drafted the spec with 43 acceptance criteria, nine design decisions with alternatives, and a breakdown into nine sub-issues with a Sprint 3 demo slice (PR #133). I posted our questions to the customer on #131. For #130 (hours on the partial-day away panel) I wrote the build plan and a draft Test Evidence table, one row per acceptance criterion.

What remains: the #130 code PR after its spec review, my OIDC sub-issue once the team assigns owners, its spec review and PR, and mutation testing with StrykerJS on one of my issues.

## What is one thing you learned about testing in your project?

Passing tests only show that the code does what the tests expect, not what the spec asks. In Sprint 2, PR #125 (waitlist) passed all 45 existing tests, yet a review found three real bugs: a blank panel on fully booked days, a six-hour hold cut to five minutes, and duplicate offers on retry. No test had checked those cases, because the tests followed the code's main path.

So for #130 I wrote the expected values from the acceptance criteria before writing any code. For example, a 14:10 to 14:50 window must print 14:10 and 14:50, not the 14:00 and 15:00 slot times.

## What is one risk to finishing your work by Nov 19, and what will you do about it?

The biggest risk is the OIDC demo. It needs five sub-issues merged in order, and one of them changes the 1,255-line `next-auth-options.ts`, where a mistake in account linking can let one user log in as another. Every sub-issue also needs a spec review and an approval before merge, so a one-day wait at each step adds up.

To reduce this, the breakdown has a merge order so that two people can work in parallel after the first PR. The account-linking code waits for the customer's answer. Until then we reject matching emails, which is safe. I will also ask for reviews on Zulip the day each PR opens.

The panel gives the reason, the public note and the redirect, but it does not say when the host is away. The attendee has to work out the hours from the gap between the slots, and a slot that straddles the leave time makes that gap wider than the window. PR #110 records this as debt it introduced.\n\nThe panel can also show the wrong entry. `AvailableTimes` renders one panel for each run of adjacent away slots, so two back-to-back entries form one run and the panel shows only the first entry. The server allows this case: `outOfOfficeCreateOrUpdate.handler.ts` rejects only an exact duplicate of start and end. With hours on the panel, that defect would also print the wrong time.\n\n### Describe the solution you would like\n\nCarry the window's start and end on each away slot that a window marks. Title: Remove unused getPartialDayOutOfOfficeRanges after the #130 away-window change

Labels: `type: improvement`, `scope: small`, `effort:low`. Milestone: Sprint 3. Assignee: zach-short.

## Summary

`getPartialDayOutOfOfficeRanges` (`packages/features/schedules/lib/date-ranges.ts:279`) has no caller outside its own tests (`date-ranges.test.ts:5`, `:1297-1376`). `getPartialDayOutOfOfficeWindows` replaced it in #104. This issue removes the dead function and moves each of its test cases onto `getPartialDayOutOfOfficeWindows`, so no coverage is lost.

This was AC9 of #130. It moved here on 2026-11-19 after the #130 spec review (dchan01-wm, 2026-11-12) pointed out that #130 would pass the 10-code-file PR limit.

## User story

As a maintainer, I want one function for partial-day out-of-office windows, so that a later change cannot fix one copy and miss the other.

## Acceptance criteria

1. `getPartialDayOutOfOfficeRanges` is deleted from `date-ranges.ts`. `git grep getPartialDayOutOfOfficeRanges` returns nothing.
2. Each of its six test cases (`date-ranges.test.ts:1297-1376`) has an equal case on `getPartialDayOutOfOfficeWindows`, with the same inputs and the same expected start and end.
3. `TZ=UTC yarn test` and `VITEST_MODE=timezone yarn test` pass with the same or more tests than before.
4. No behavior changes: no file outside `date-ranges.ts` and `date-ranges.test.ts` is edited.

## Out of scope

Any change to `getPartialDayOutOfOfficeWindows` itself; the #130 panel work.

=== PR153 body heads
3:## What this does
7:## Design
9:**How the window reaches the panel.** `slots.ts` already copies the entry's data onto each away slot. It now also copies the window's ISO start and end into two optional fields, `outOfOfficeStart` and `outOfOfficeEnd`. Only a window has a `start`, so the fields are set behind a `"start" in` check and the slots of a whole-day entry get neither. `findOutOfOfficeForSlot` now declares that it can return an `IOutOfOfficeWindow`, which is what it returned at runtime already. The date record's top-level copy of the first window (`getUserAvailability.ts`, `acc[date] = { ...entryData, windows: [record] }`) is built from the entry data alone, so it has no `start` and cannot put the fields on another slot.
13:**Where one panel ends and the next starts.** `AvailableTimes` starts a new panel when the slot's `outOfOfficeStart` or `outOfOfficeEnd` differs from the previous away slot. The same rule decides the all-away layout: when every slot is away for the same window (or for a whole-day entry, where both fields are absent), the day keeps the single whole-day panel. When two windows cover the day, the day goes through the normal list and gets one panel per window. Comparing reason and note was rejected because two entries with the same reason would merge. One panel that lists every window was rejected because a panel has one redirect button.
15:**The formatter.** `formatAwayWindow(startIso, endIso, timeZone, timeFormat, locale)` in `apps/web/modules/bookings/lib/formatAwayWindow.ts` is a pure function. It uses Day.js for the times because the result depends on the zone's offset at each instant, and it uses the same format strings as the slot buttons (`h:mma`, `HH:mm`). When the two instants are on different dates in the booker's zone, each time gets its date from `Intl.DateTimeFormat` with the booker's locale (month short, day numeric), for example "Oct 8, 22:00" in `en` and "8 Oct, 22:00" in `en-GB`. A window that ends exactly at the booker's midnight counts as two dates, because midnight is the first instant of the next date.
17:**The 12-hour and 24-hour toggle.** `AvailableTimeSlots` hid the toggle on a day where every slot is away. A day covered by windows now prints hours, so the toggle stays. It is hidden only when every slot is away and no panel has hours (`dayPrintsNoTimes`).
19:**Types.** `SlotInfo` (`packages/features/calendars/lib/types.ts`) and the booker's slot type (`IGetAvailableSlots` in `useAvailableTimeSlots.ts`, which is the declared return type of the tRPC schedule query) both list `notes`, `outOfOfficeStart` and `outOfOfficeEnd`. `AvailableTimes.test.tsx` no longer widens the type locally.

## Requirements and Design

zach-short

- **#130, how the hours reach the panel.** `slots.ts` already copied the out-of-office entry's reason and note onto each away slot. It now copies the window's start and end as two optional fields too. A second lookup from the booker was rejected because the slot already has the data and a second source could disagree with it.
- **#130, where one panel ends and the next starts.** A new panel starts when the window's start or end differs from the previous away slot. Comparing reason and note was rejected because two entries with the same reason would merge. One panel that lists every window was rejected because a panel has one redirect button.
- **#130, the formatter.** `formatAwayWindow` is a pure function with the same format strings as the slot buttons. When the window crosses midnight in the attendee's zone, each time gets its date. A 14:10 to 14:50 window prints 14:10 and 14:50, not the 14:00 and 15:00 slot times.
- **#130, scope change after the spec review.** The reviewer (dchan01-wm, 2026-11-12) pointed out that removing the dead function `getPartialDayOutOfOfficeRanges` would take the PR past the 10-file limit. That criterion moved to a separate hardening issue.
- **#131, OIDC spec.** The spec has the acceptance criteria, the edge cases and eleven design decisions with their rejected alternatives (`specs/oidc-sign-in/` in draft PR #133). We posted 13 questions on #131. The customer answered all of them on 2026-11-12, and the answers are recorded in the criteria. Two of them (the password-login switch and accepting the provider's MFA) became Sprint 4 work.
- **#136, the user link.** A user is linked to a provider through the existing `Account` row with `provider = "oidc-<id>"`, not through a new join table, so NextAuth's account lookup works unchanged.
- **#136, the secret.** The table stores only the ciphertext of the client secret. One repository method returns it, and no other method selects it. A duplicate issuer and client ID becomes a `BadRequest` error built from the issuer alone, because the raw Prisma error can print the failed write, which holds the ciphertext.
- Diagrams for #130 (class and sequence): `docs/sprint3/diagrams/130-zach-short.md` in PR #153.

## Test Strategy

zach-short

- **#130.** Expected values were written from the acceptance criteria before the code. Three levels:
  - Unit tests on the pure formatter `formatAwayWindow`: 12-hour and 24-hour formats, a window that crosses midnight in the attendee's zone, a window that ends exactly at midnight, DST start and end, and two locales.
  - Unit tests on `slots.ts`: a window sets both new fields on the slots it marks, and a whole-day entry sets neither.
  - Component tests on `AvailableTimes` and `AvailableTimeSlots`: one panel per window, two panels for back-to-back entries, the whole-day layout unchanged, and the time format toggle on five kinds of day.
  - Not tested automatically: the page in a real browser in two time zones. The PR body says so.
- **#136.** 23 unit tests on the repository with a mocked Prisma client, as the issue asks. They check the `select` of every read (no method except one may select the secret), the conversion of the duplicate and not-found errors, and that the delete runs in one transaction. They do not prove that Postgres enforces the unique pair or the rollback. The migration was not run on a real database.
- **Gates.** CI did not run the type check or the tests on any code PR this sprint, because the "Prepare" job fails at the Playwright install. I ran both locally. import { getRunningLateService } from "@calcom/features/bookings/di/RunningLateService.container";
import { checkRateLimitAndThrowError } from "@calcom/lib/checkRateLimitAndThrowError";
import { HttpError } from "@calcom/lib/http-error";
import { TRPCError } from "@trpc/server";
import type { TrpcSessionUser } from "../../../types";
import type { TRunningLateInputSchema } from "./runningLate.schema";

type RunningLateOptions = {
  ctx: {
    user: NonNullable<TrpcSessionUser>;
  };
  input: TRunningLateInputSchema;
};

export const runningLateHandler = async ({ ctx, input }: RunningLateOptions) => {
  await checkRunningLateRateLimit({ userId: ctx.user.id, bookingId: input.bookingId });

  const runningLateService = getRunningLateService();
  return runningLateService.sendNotice({
    bookingId: input.bookingId,
    userId: ctx.user.id,
    delayMinutes: input.delayMinutes,
    message: input.message,
  });
};

async function checkRunningLateRateLimit({ userId, bookingId }: { userId: number; bookingId: number }) {
  try {
    // Keyed by user as well as booking so a non-host hitting this endpoint can't use up the host's quota
    await checkRateLimitAndThrowError({
      rateLimitingType: "runningLate",
      identifier: `runningLate:${userId}:${bookingId}`,
    });
  } catch (error) {
    // errorConversionMiddleware only converts ErrorWithCode, so an HttpError would reach the client as a 500
    if (error instanceof HttpError && error.statusCode === 429) {
      throw new TRPCError({ code: "TOO_MANY_REQUESTS", message: error.message, cause: error });
    }
    throw error;
  }
}
=== body
## Design 
*Note: Design documentation included as per project requirements.*

*   **Decision**: Only the booking's organizer can send a running late notice. The server checks that the logged-in user's id matches the booking's `userId` (`RunningLateService.sendNotice`) and rejects everyone else with Forbidden. The bookings list uses the same rule to decide whether to show the action (`getRunningLateAction`).
*   **Alternatives considered**: 1. Reusing the existing cancellation logic, which accepts a client-provided email. 2. Letting anyone who can see the booking send it, including co-hosts, round-robin hosts and team admins. 3. Blocking the action entirely for everyone.
*   **Rationale**: The organizer is the person attendees are waiting for, so they're the one who knows they are late. Co-hosts and admins can see the booking but aren't necessarily the one running late. The check uses the server session, so attendees can't fake it, whereas reusing the cancellation logic would let an attendee spoof the host's email.
*   **Consequences**: Attendees, co-hosts and admins can't send notices, even if one of them is actually running late. Hosts who are logged out must log in first.

#### Open questions from #137

*   **Team events:** only the booking's organizer (`booking.userId`) can send a notice. For collective events, the other hosts are stored as attendees (`createBooking.ts:154-159`), so they can't send one.
*   **Notifying others:** the organizer doesn't get a copy. Because co-hosts on a collective event are stored as attendees, they do get the "X is running late" email (`RunningLateService.test.ts` › skips the sender regardless of email casing and de-duplicates attendees).
*   **Repeat notices:** each notice is a new email; it doesn't replace an earlier one. A host can send at most 1 notice per booking every 5 minutes (a dedicated `runningLate` Unkey rate-limit tier keyed by user and booking). After that they see a "please wait" toast.
*   **Language:** each attendee gets the email in their own locale and time zone.

## Tech Debt

**Introduced:**
- **The rate limit depends on Unkey, and notices aren't recorded.** Repeat notices are capped at 1 per booking every 5 minutes per host, but the limiter allows everything when `UNKEY_ROOT_KEY` isn't set (`packages/lib/rateLimit.ts`), so local and self-hosted setups without Unkey have no cap. Nothing stores that a notice was sent; an audit-log entry would need a schema change, which was out of scope for this issue.
- **The toast confirms the notice was sent, not delivered.** `BaseEmail.sendEmail` logs and swallows SMTP errors and always resolves, so the service can't tell whether an email was delivered. The toast says the notice was sent, with no count, and the host isn't told if an attendee missed it. Failures before sending (translations, building the email) are logged by `RunningLateService`, and the other attendees still get theirs.
- **No component test for `RunningLateDialog.tsx`.** The delay picker and toasts are only checked by hand. The rules behind them are covered by the schema and service tests.
- **Per-issue mutation config at the repo root.** `stryker.137.config.mjs` and `vitest.stryker-137.config.mts` follow the existing per-issue pattern (`stryker.138.config.mjs`), which adds a root file pair for each issue.

**Encountered:**
- **The cancellation flow trusts a client-provided email to identify the host.** We didn't reuse it. The running late check uses the server session instead (see Design). The cancellation flow itself is unchanged because fixing it is outside this issue.
- **Stryker 10 needs Node 22, and the project default here was Node 20.** We ran it with `nvm exec 22` rather than changing the project's Node version.


=== comment
Thanks for the review. All four items and the minor notes are addressed in three commits:

1. **Sent count counted failed emails as sent:** 205b8466c3. `sendNotice` now returns `recipientCount` (attendees we tried to notify), and the toast says "Running late notice sent to your attendees" without a count. The failure test now makes `getTranslation` reject instead of `sendEmail`, which matches what can actually reach `allSettled`. I also corrected the mutation write-up: the `log.error` only covers failures before the send, since `BaseEmail` swallows SMTP errors itself.
2. **Who the host is:** the Design section now has an "Open questions from #137" part answering Team events (organizer only; co-hosts on collective events are stored as attendees) and Notifying others (organizer gets no copy, co-hosts do).
3. **Repeat notices:** 67fc78fd61. A new `runningLate` Unkey tier allows 1 notice every 5 minutes, keyed by user and booking so a non-host can't use up the host's quota. `checkRateLimitAndThrowError` throws `HttpError`, which `errorConversionMiddleware` doesn't convert, so the handler maps the 429 to `TOO_MANY_REQUESTS`. New `runningLate.handler.test.ts` covers it. Tech Debt notes that the limiter is a no-op without `UNKEY_ROOT_KEY`.
4. **Title / Tech Debt / draft:** the title is now `feat(bookings): add running late notice for hosts`, Tech Debt is updated for the two changes above, and the PR is back in draft.

**Minor, translated errors:** 99211bc250. The dialog maps the tRPC error code to translated keys instead of showing `error.message`.

Local run at `99211bc`: 5 files, 106 tests passed. `yarn type-check:ci --force` passes. I didn't re-run Stryker, so the recorded scores are from `974a231`.

Title: Remove unused getPartialDayOutOfOfficeRanges after the #130 away-window change
